extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and emerging writers seeking craft, submission, and publishing advice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing, revising, researching, querying agents, and selecting contests/workshops—aimed at writers preparing manuscripts for submission and publication. Includes agent preferences and practical submission strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage readers on first pages / page-one importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The first several pages of your manuscript are of the highest importance; agents and editors size up your writing within a minute and if you don't have their attention on Page 1, they stop reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overused techniques or cliches; the site promotes webinars such as “Your Story’s First Pages: How to Engage the Reader” (which includes a critique of the first 500 words) to help ensure early pages hook readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough research to achieve authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: You can’t do too much research. Time spent gathering intelligence is seldom wasted; small authentic details give scenes a ring of authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anecdote: a detail about a scuba diver’s blood appearing green at depth convinced a professor the author had sensory knowledge. Seek out specific, believable details that support scenes and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and rewriting are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing is rewriting. After the words are down on paper, you must begin the important process of honing, revising, and rewriting to eliminate weak writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish your words, eliminate all needless elements that can slow a manuscript down. The site warns that most work gets rejected simply because the manuscript is not where it needs to be in terms of quality; consider revision-focused webinars and personalized critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query in tiers (tiered querying strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Query in tiers: identify your top five dream agents, send initial queries to them and then wait; only move on to tier two when you’ve exhausted tier one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical strategy is recommended to avoid prematurely accepting representation and to prioritize sending to best-fit agents first ('rinse and repeat' for subsequent tiers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand agent–author relationship: agent works for you
rubrics_metrics.description: An agent offers a service—selling your writing to editors—in exchange for a fee. Your agent works for you; the relationship is a partnership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should treat the relationship as collaborative: you hire an agent, they know the publishing world, but they make no decisions without you and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow agent-specific genre and submission preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents list explicit preferences about genres, age categories, themes, and exclusions; you should target queries only to agents who state they seek your kind of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: Brittany Howard seeks YA (high fantasy to paranormal to soft sci-fi to contemporary), likes strong voice for MG, is selective on picture books, and favors adult fiction that’s 'a romance at heart' for certain subgenres; Susan Hawk seeks books for children of all ages (YA, MG, picture books, fiction and nonfiction); Margaret Bail seeks adult fiction only (romance, SF, thrillers, action/adventure, historical, Western, certain fantasy) and explicitly does NOT seek YA, MG, children's, steampunk, Christian/religious, chick lit, poetry, or screenplays. Do not query agents outside their stated lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter contests aligned with the contest’s niche
rubrics_metrics.description: Many recurring contests keep the same entry mechanics but change the niche; each contest is focused around a specific category or two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose contests that match your genre/category (e.g., a Dear Lucky Agent contest focused on YA and sci-fi). Check contest deadlines and rules before entering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek professional critique via webinars and workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Webinars and workshops that include personalized critiques (e.g., critique of first 500 words, individualized query critiques) are recommended for improving submission materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these opportunities to get targeted feedback on openings, queries, and revision needs; advertised offerings include first-page critiques and query critiques as part of webinar enrollment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong voice is essential for middle grade and younger categories
rubrics_metrics.description: For middle grade (and many YA) submissions, agents emphasize that a strong narrative voice is a must.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agent listings on the page repeatedly note 'strong voice is MUST' for MG; ensure manuscripts for younger readers demonstrate a clear, compelling voice appropriate to the age category.
